scheme.model_answer: To check that the program accepts ordinary data and produces the correct results.

questions.title: Why boundary data
questions.text: Explain why boundary data is used in testing.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Checks that the values at the limits are accepted / values just outside rejected (1)
- finds off-by-one errors in comparisons such as < instead of <= (1)
scheme.model_answer: It checks the program accepts the exact limits and rejects values just outside them, which finds off-by-one mistakes such as using < instead of <=.

Extreme: 5

questions.title: Finding the error
questions.text:
The code should accept marks from 0 to 100.

Identify a test value that shows the error, the result it gives, and the correction.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Boundary value 0 or 100 (1)
- is rejected / shows "Mark must be 0-100" although it is valid (1)
- change to mark >= 0 and mark <= 100 (1)
scheme.model_answer: Test 100: the program prints "Mark must be 0-100" although 100 is valid. Correct the condition to mark >= 0 and mark <= 100.

questions.title: Purpose of erroneous data
questions.text: Explain the purpose of testing a program with erroneous data.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Checks that invalid data is rejected / validation works (1)
- program does not crash and gives a suitable error message (1)
scheme.model_answer: To make sure invalid data is rejected by the validation, and that the program shows an error message instead of crashing.

| Type | Value | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| Normal | Pass1234w (9) | Accepted |
| Boundary | Pass1234 (8) | Accepted |

options.content: Name of the user who will buy the program

scheme.mark_scheme: A, C, D
scheme.explanation: The actual result is filled in during testing.

questions.title: Expected results
questions.text: Explain why the expected result of each test is written **before** the program is tested.

scheme.mark_scheme: So the actual result can be compared with it to decide pass / fail (1); writing it afterwards risks copying a wrong output as correct (1)
scheme.model_answer: So that the actual output can be compared with it; if it were written afterwards, a wrong result might simply be copied as the expected one.

questions.title: A failed test
questions.text: Test 5 (an empty field) made the program crash. Describe what the programmer should do next.

scheme.mark_scheme: Record the actual result / mark as failed (1); find the cause and correct the code, e.g. add a presence check (1); re-run the failed test and the earlier tests (regression testing) (1)
scheme.model_answer: Record that the test failed, add a presence check so empty input gives an error message, then run test 5 again and repeat the other tests to check nothing else broke.

questions.title: Black-box testing
questions.text: In black-box testing the tester chooses test data by reading the program code.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: That is white-box testing; black-box testing only checks inputs and outputs against the requirements.

questions.title: Only normal data
questions.text: A programmer tested a registration form only with normal data and every test passed. Explain why the program may still contain errors.

scheme.mark_scheme: Boundary errors (wrong < / <=) are not found without boundary data (1); validation errors / crashes with invalid input are not found without erroneous data (1)
scheme.model_answer: Normal data does not test the limits, so off-by-one errors stay hidden, and it does not check that invalid input is rejected, so the program might accept wrong data or crash.

questions.title: Exam marks program
questions.text: A teacher's program asks for a test mark, which must be a **whole number from 0 to 40**, and outputs "Saved" or an error message.

parts.title: Test plan
parts.text: Complete the test plan with two values of each type and the expected result.

scheme.mark_scheme: 1 mark per row with correct value and expected result: normal 1–39 → Saved; boundary 0 and 40 → Saved (or −1 / 41 → error); erroneous e.g. 55, −5, "ten", 20.5, blank → error message. Two different erroneous kinds expected for both marks.
scheme.model_answer:
| Type | Value | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| Normal | 25 | Saved |
| Normal | 12 | Saved |
| Boundary | 0 | Saved |
| Boundary | 40 | Saved |
| Erroneous | 47 | Error message |
| Erroneous | ten | Error message |

parts.title: Boundary purpose
parts.text: Explain why the teacher should test the values 0 and 40.

scheme.mark_scheme: They are the limits of the valid range / boundary data (1); check comparisons are correct, e.g. <= not < / off-by-one errors (1)
scheme.model_answer: 0 and 40 are the limits, so testing them shows whether the conditions use <= and >= correctly; an off-by-one error would reject them.

parts.title: Erroneous purpose
parts.text: Explain why the value "ten" is used in testing and what the program should do with it.

scheme.mark_scheme: Erroneous data of the wrong type (1); checks the program does not crash / type check works (1); should reject it and display an error message asking for a number (1)
scheme.model_answer: "ten" is erroneous data of the wrong type; it checks the program does not crash when text is entered. It should reject it and ask the teacher to enter a number.

summary: Why programs are tested, the types of test data — normal, boundary (extreme) and erroneous (abnormal) — how to choose test values for ranges, lengths, choices, formats and several inputs, writing and using a test plan with expected and actual results, dry runs and trace tables, black-box and white-box testing, and what to do when a test fails.

blocks.content: Running a program with **carefully chosen data** to check that it **works correctly**, **meets the requirements** and **does not crash** — and to **find and remove errors** before the program is used for real.

items.title: What testing checks
items.content:
- The program gives **correct results** for valid input.
- It works at the **limits** of what is allowed.
- It **rejects** invalid input with a **clear error message** instead of crashing.
- It meets the **user requirements** of the new system.

items.title: Why it matters
items.content:
- Errors found **early** are cheaper and easier to fix.
- A program with errors can give **wrong results** (wrong marks, wrong bills) and lose **data** or **trust**.
- Testing gives **evidence** that the system works — required in the project documentation.

blocks.title: Types of test data at a glance
rows: Data at the **edges** of the valid range — the largest and smallest accepted values (and the values **just outside** them)
Data that **should be rejected**: out of range, wrong type, wrong format, missing
**Rejected** with an error message; no crash

blocks.content: Typical, **sensible data that the program should accept** and process correctly — values well **inside** the valid range and of the correct type.

items.title: Purpose
items.content: - To check that the program gives the **correct results** for ordinary input — the calculations, decisions and outputs are right.

items.title: How to choose normal data
items.content:
- Pick **several** values from the **middle** of the range, not at the edges.
- Work out the **expected result** **before** running the test (by hand or with a calculator).
- Include values that take **different paths** through the program (each branch of an IF).

blocks.title: Normal data for a ticket price program
blocks.content:
Rule: age 0–17 pays 1500 ₸, age 18–64 pays 3000 ₸, age 65–120 pays 1000 ₸.
Normal test data: **10** → 1500 ₸, **35** → 3000 ₸, **70** → 1000 ₸ (one value for **each** branch).

Data **at the edges of the valid range** — the **largest and smallest values that should be accepted**. Many teachers and mark schemes also test the values **just outside** the limits, which must be rejected.

items.title: Purpose
items.content:
- To check that comparisons such as `<` and `<=`, `>` and `>=` are written correctly — **off-by-one errors** are very common.
- To check that the program does not reject the **limits** themselves.

items.title: How to choose boundary data
items.content:
- Read the **exact limits** from the question.
- Test **each limit**: the lowest and the highest valid value.
- Optionally test **just below** the lowest and **just above** the highest value (these are rejected).
- For **whole numbers** "just outside" means ±1; for decimals use the smallest step, e.g. 100.1.

blocks.title: Boundary data for a mark from 0 to 100
blocks.content:
| Value | Accepted? | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **0** | Yes | Lowest valid value |
| **100** | Yes | Highest valid value |
| −1 | No | Just below the range |
| 101 | No | Just above the range |

blocks.title: Extreme data in NIS mark schemes
blocks.content: For a variable that may only be **3, 4 or 5** (e.g. midfielders in a football formation), the **extreme** values are **3 and 5** — the smallest and largest accepted values. Erroneous data is any other number (2, 6, 9) or a non-numeric value.

mark = int(input("Mark: "))
if mark > 0 and mark < 100:        # bug: should be >= 0 and <= 100
    print("Mark saved")
else:
    print("Mark must be 0–100")
# Test 0   → "Mark must be 0–100"   ✗ expected "Mark saved"
# Test 100 → "Mark must be 0–100"   ✗ expected "Mark saved"
# Normal data such as 45 would NOT have found this error.
blocks.caption: An off-by-one error found with boundary data

blocks.content: Data that **should be rejected** by the program: **outside the range**, of the **wrong data type**, in the **wrong format**, too **long / short**, or **missing**.

items.title: Purpose
items.content:
- To check that **validation** works — invalid data is **not accepted** or saved.
- To check that the program **does not crash** and gives a **suitable error message**, so the user can correct the input.

items.title: Kinds of erroneous data
items.content:
- **Out of range**: −20, 250 for a mark 0–100.
- **Wrong type**: "abc", 45.5 when a whole number is required.
- **Wrong format**: an e-mail without "@", a date 31/02/2026.
- **Wrong length**: a 3-character password when at least 8 are needed.
- **Missing**: an empty field.

blocks.title: Choosing test data for different rules
Choosing test data: a mark must be a whole number from 0 to 100
blocks.content:
| Type | Test values | Expected result |
|---|---|---|
| Normal | 45, 73 | Accepted |
| Boundary | 0, 100 (accepted); −1, 101 (rejected) | As stated |
| Erroneous | −20, 250, "abc", empty, 45.5 | Rejected with an error message |

A table, written **before** testing, that lists each **test**, its **purpose**, the **test data**, the **type** of data and the **expected result**. During testing the **actual result** is recorded and compared.

blocks.title: What to do when a test fails
items: Record the **actual result** and mark the test as **failed**.
Find the **cause** — trace the code or use a debugger.
**Re-run** the failed test **and** the earlier tests (**regression testing**) to make sure nothing else has broken.

items.title: Dry run and trace table
items.content:
- Following the code **by hand** with test data, writing the value of each variable after every step in a **trace table**.
- Finds **logic errors** before the program is run.

items.title: Black-box testing
items.content: - Tests **inputs and outputs** against the requirements **without looking at the code** — normal, boundary and erroneous data.

items.title: White-box testing
items.content: - Tests are chosen **from the code**, so that **every branch and loop** is executed at least once.

items.title: Testing by users
items.content: - **Alpha** testing by the developers' team; **beta** testing by real users before release; **acceptance** testing by the client.

blocks.title: A dry run with a trace table
blocks.content:
```python
total = 0
for n in [4, -1, 6]:
    if n > 0:
        total = total + n
print(total)
```
| n | n > 0 | total |
|---|---|---|
| — | — | 0 |
| 4 | True | 4 |
| −1 | False | 4 |
| 6 | True | 10 |

Output **10** — matches the expected result (sum of the positive numbers).

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: A program accepts the number of midfielders mid = 3, 4 or 5. Give examples of data that test the variable mid. [2]**
Extreme: **3** (or 5) (1); erroneous: any number that is not 3, 4 or 5, e.g. **9**, or a non-numeric value (1).

**Q: A field accepts a whole number of tickets from 1 to 10. Complete a test plan with one normal, one boundary and one erroneous value. [3]**
Normal **5** → accepted (1); boundary **10** → accepted (1); erroneous **15** / "two" → rejected with an error message (1).

**Q: Explain why boundary data is used in testing. [2]**
It checks the program accepts the values **at the limits** (1) and finds **off-by-one errors** in comparisons such as `<` instead of `<=` (1).

**Q: Explain why expected results are written before testing. [2]**
So that the **actual result** can be **compared** with them (1) and errors noticed; working out the result after the run may just copy a wrong output (1).

- Giving a **boundary** value that is not the exact limit (e.g. 98 for a range 0–100).
- Giving only **one** erroneous value when several kinds exist (range, type, missing).
- Forgetting the **expected result** — every test needs one.
- Calling "−1" normal data for a range 0–100 — it is **boundary (just outside)** or **erroneous**.
- Testing only with normal data — it does **not** find off-by-one or validation errors.
